episodes.213972: Diurnally driven thunderstorm activity enhanced by an approaching upper low and fueled by abundant monsoonal moisture yielded heavy rain producing thunderstorms over the burn scars surrounding the Village of Ruidoso on the 20th. Flash flooding impacted areas just down stream of the Salt burn scar near Hollywood and Ruidoso Downs, and the South Fork burn scar north of Ruidoso near Alto. Late evening thunderstorms produced brief heavy rain that resulted in flash flooding in the town of Aztec, NM. The upper low continued toward the NM and AZ border on the 21st producing more rounds of afternoon and evening thunderstorm activity to areas along and west of the central mountain chain. A few of these thunderstorms produced heavy rain reaching up to 2 inches, resulting in considerable flash flooding impacts to Gallup and Zuni Pueblo. Heavy street flooding impacted travel across the area and also infiltrated the ground floor of Rehoboth McKinley Christian Hospital in Gallup, NM. Evacuations were ordered from severe flash flooding across portions of the Zuni Pueblo. The upper low migrated northward toward the Four Corners area and eastern UT, with abundant monsoonal moisture still funneling into western NM. This yielded another day of scattered to numerous afternoon thunderstorms along and west of the Continental Divide through western NM. These storms exacerbated ongoing flooding issues in Gallup and Zuni Pueblo, and producing isolated flooding impacts on the western edge of the Acoma Pueblo near the El Malpais Ranger Station.
episodes.214022: Thunderstorms developed ahead of a warm front across north-central Wisconsin during the mid-afternoon on Monday (7/20), producing hail up to quarter size. Additional thunderstorms developed later in the afternoon and into the evening on Monday (7/20) with a cold front across central and east-central Wisconsin.  These storms produced several weak tornadoes, which were viewed by several storm chasers, and damaging winds.
episodes.214070: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours of July 19, 2026. An abundant amount of atmospheric moisture allowed these thunderstorms to produce another round of heavy rain. The most significant flooding was reported in southern Lawrence County and Cookeville where several area roadways were reported flooded and impassable.
episodes.214214: A few thunderstorms developed along a stationary front during the late afternoon into early evening. One storm became severe, producing damaging winds.
episodes.214290: Moisture on the eastern periphery TS Bertha in the northern Gulf streamed into the area as weak troughing persisted. Robust heating in this moisture rich environment brought strong instability and an isolated severe storm in Clarendon County which caused isolated tree damage.
episodes.214552: Monsoon storms formed during the afternoon of July 20th bringing severe winds and heavy rain with flash flooding, especially to the Prescott Valley area. Some activity continued into the early morning hours of July 21st in the Page area.
episodes.214952: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced several wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.215159: A tropical upper tropospheric trough (TUTT) across south Florida on July 16th shifted northwestward and closed off into an upper low over the northeastern Gulf on July 17th. The combination of deep tropical moisture and mid level cooler air overspread into northern Florida and Georgia supporting numerous showers and thunderstorms each afternoon and evening developing along the inland-moving sea breezes. A broad surface low then developed under the upper low in the northeastern Gulf and gradually deepened into Invest 91 on July 18th and then strengthened into Tropical Depression 2 on July 19th. Showers and thunderstorms rotated around the eastern side of the system shifting northward up the Florida peninsula July 19th into July 20th. A few strong to severe storms developed as the outer rainbands from TD 2 interacted with the sea breeze and outflow boundaries. On July 20th, mid-level drier air filtered into the area from the south triggering some stronger downbursts.
episodes.215286: A stagnant ridge of high pressure over the Rockies lead to an influx of monsoon moisture into southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska. As a result, thunderstorms produced heavy rain and strong winds.
episodes.215516: A stalled frontal boundary bisected Eastern North Carolina through the overnight hours on July nineteenth. This front combined with the sea breeze and ample instability to promote the development of thunderstorm clusters during the afternoon and evening hours on July nineteenth. A few of these storms became strong to severe in nature bringing damaging wind gusts and even a report of a waterspout to areas along and north of the Neuse River.
episodes.215517: A stalled front remained around the Albemarle Sound through the day on July twentieth. With ample instability in place and the stalled front becoming the focus for surface convergence, clusters of thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours around and north of the Albemarle Sound and then tracked east-southeastwards through the evening. A few of these storms became strong in nature bringing isolated strong wind gusts to the northern sounds and Pamlico Sound.
episodes.215590: A cluster of thunderstorms developed along a northward moving outflow boundary in the early evening hours across southeast Georgia. The storms became strong enough to produce a few damaging wind gusts across interior southeast Georgia.
episodes.215942: A tropical upper tropospheric trough (TUTT) across south Florida on July 16th shifted northwestward and closed off into an upper low over the northeastern Gulf on July 17th. The combination of deep tropical moisture and mid level cooler air overspread into northern Florida and Georgia supporting numerous showers and thunderstorms each afternoon and evening developing along the inland-moving sea breezes. A broad surface low then developed under the upper low in the northeastern Gulf and gradually deepened into Invest 91 on July 18th and then strengthened into Tropical Depression 2 on July 19th. Showers and thunderstorms rotated around the eastern side of the system shifting northward up the Florida peninsula July 19th into July 20th. A few strong to severe storms developed as the outer rainbands from TD 2 interacted with the sea breeze and outflow boundaries. On July 20th, mid-level drier air filtered into the area from the south triggering some stronger downbursts.
episodes.215958: A monsoonal pattern persisted onward through mid July, resulting in more instances of thunderstorm winds and flash flooding.
episodes.216161: Outer convective bands along the eastern semi-circle of Tropical Depression Two (precursor to Tropical Storm Bertha) over the northeastern Gulf produce numerous strong marine wind gusts along the western Florida peninsula coast from southwest Florida northward across west central Florida and the Nature Coast.
episodes.216187: A southward moving cold front from the Middle Atlantic region produced showers and storms across central North Carolina during the late afternoon and evening hours. Storms started across the northern Piedmont and Coastal Plain, eventually shifting into the southern Piedmont and Sandhills during the late evening and early overnight hours.
episodes.216188: A stalled frontal boundary draped mainly along the US Highway 64 corridor led to the development of afternoon and evening showers and storms. The front gradually lifted north into the next day, however storms additionally developed over the Piedmont and Coastal Plain of central NC, producing several damaging wind reports.
episodes.216252: Two different lines of thunderstorms with damaging winds moved through eastern IA on Monday, bringing up to 3.5 inches of rain and a few significant gusts of 70-74 mph.
episodes.216260: Two lines of storms with damaging winds moved through western IL on Monday, bringing up to 3.5 inches of rain and a few significant gusts of 70-74 mph.
episodes.216297: Isolated strong thunderstorms produced high winds in central and north central South Dakota during the evening of July 19. ||In Campbell County, the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station two miles north of Herreid measured an extreme wind gust of 87 mph. The same storm system previously struck Mobridge, where the Mobridge Regional Airport ASOS recorded a 64 mph (56 knots) gust, downing tree branches and damaging the screen support structures at the Mobridge Pheasant Drive-In.||In central South Dakota, thunderstorm wind gusts of 62 mph were recorded on a public mesonet station near Presho and the South Dakota State University mesonet station 6 miles south southeast of Kennebec in central South Dakota.
episodes.216341: An upper level shortwave moved over a very hot and humid airmass, leading to scattered thunderstorms developing along a surface trough in central North Dakota. The main threat with these supercell thunderstorms was large hail, with the largest hail of 2 inches in diameter reported south of Dawson in Kidder County. There were also a few reports of damaging thunderstorm wind gusts as the storms moved east into south central North Dakota and the southern James River Valley. The strongest reported wind gust was 72 mph at the NDAWN station near Wirch in McIntosh County.
episodes.216587: Broad cyclonic flow aloft over the eastern Gulf and Florida peninsula coupled with a developing surface low over the eastern Gulf that would become Tropical Storm Bertha created a favorable convective environment that produced waterspouts near Punta Rassa and Bradenton Beach, and strong marine wind gusts over the Tampa Bay waters.
episodes.216733: An upper high was located over Colorado with northeast flow over southern New Mexico. Residual monsoonal moisture was still in the area and allowed for heavy rain and flash flooding to occur around Las Cruces and a severe thunderstorm moved through the Lordsburg Playa.
episodes.216764: An area of low pressure over the northeastern Gulf became Tropical Depression Two on July 19th as its surface circulation and associated convection gradually became better organized. The depression remained broad and relatively weak, with scattered thunderstorms that extended far west of the circulation center. Those storms affected local coastal waters.
episodes.216776: A severe storm from south central South Dakota moved slowly eastward into Gregory County during the early evening. An increasingly unfavorable air mass caused the storm to weaken quickly, but an extended period of severe wind gusts occurred before the storm dissipated.
episodes.216779: An upper high was located over the High Plains while a weak upper low developed just south of the border in Mexico. Deep monsoonal moisture remained over the region.  A convergent area setup along the NM/Mexico border region which helped storms to stall out and bring widespread flash flooding to Luna county with additional flash flooding in Las Cruces and northeast Otero county.
episodes.216842: During the evening hours on July 20th, a shower took on supercellular characteristics and produced an EF-0 tornado south of Kellogg in Wabasha County. This tornado resulted in minor damage at a farmstead during its short duration.
episodes.216843: During the early afternoon hours on July 20th, a cluster of severe storms moved through portions of Mitchell and Floyd counties. The severe wind gusts produced by this complex of storms resulted in multiple vehicles being overturned, with one occupant receiving non-life threatening injuries.
episodes.217054: A severe thunderstorm complex tracked into far southeast ND from central and south central ND, producing damaging winds in southwest Sargent County, ND.
episodes.217075: A strong shortwave trough moved across the Upper Great Lakes brining a series of strong to severe thunderstorms to Lake Superior.
episodes.217129: A strong shortwave trough moved across the Upper Great Lakes bringing a series of strong to severe thunderstorms to the Upper Peninsula on July 20th.  Multiple rounds of thunderstorms occurred with severe thunderstorms in the morning hours and again in the late afternoon with discrete, supercell thunderstorms developing over the central portion of the U.P. A total of 3 tornadoes occurred.
episodes.217157: Isolated thunderstorms and storm clusters moved into upstate South Carolina from North Carolina during the evening. One of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Spartanburg County.
episodes.217158: Isolated thunderstorms and storm clusters developed over the North Carolina Piedmont during the late afternoon and evening. One of the storms produced a small area of damaging wind gusts in Davie County.

episodes.217227: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along an outflow boundary across West Tennessee during the evening hours of July 19, 2026. Precipitable water values over 2 inches combined with MUCAPEs above 1000 J/kg, provided support for very heavy rainfall across parts of West Tennessee, including the city of Jackson.
episodes.217301: Locally heavy rainfall in Cochise county led to road closures.
episodes.217494: A strong low-pressure system originating in the Bering Sea moved across mainland Alaska in mid-to-late July 2026, bringing multiple rounds of anomalous, heavy rainfall to Southcentral Alaska that approached record levels for the month. Between July 13 and July 23, persistent wet conditions saturated the region, with the heaviest precipitation focused over the Talkeetna Mountains and the Susitna Valley. The Talkeetna River Basin received 4 to 6 inches of rain, or a 5- to 10-year average recurrence interval. Meanwhile the Yentna Basin saw 10-day totals of 6 to 8 inches. This excessive runoff caused fast-responding rivers and streams to swell, leading to moderate flooding, severe riverbank erosion, road washouts, and a local emergency disaster declaration by the Matanuska-Susitna Borough Assembly.

Three rounds of heavy rainfall over a 10-day period resulted in moderate flooding on the Yentna River at Lake Creek. During this event, moderate flooding impacted numerous lodges and properties in the Lake Creek area, with reports of up to 1 foot of water inside structures. High-water marks at McDougal Lodge were estimated to be nearly 3 feet lower than the record flood of August 2025, resulting in substantially less severe structural impacts than the previous year.   Between July 13 and July 23, the Yentna Basin received 6 to 8 inches of rainfall, representing a 10- to 25-year return interval for 10-day precipitation totals. This series of storms caused three distinct river crests: the first storm produced 2 to 3 inches of rain and a crest of 21.17 feet on July 15; a second storm brought an additional 2 to 4 inches of rain, cresting at 21.89 feet on July 21; and a final storm dropped around 2 inches of rain, pushing the river to a moderate flood crest of 21.95 feet on July 23.
